doc.title: Steve Wilson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 25, 2002

chapter: Richmond and arriving in New York
title: Non-music jobs and keeping perspective
summary: Hospital stock clerk, shoe salesman and the dishwashing job he quit for a disco band.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: Did you have to work non-music jobs during this time in New York?

Not in New York. While I was in school I did work a non-music job, I worked in a hospital as a stock clerk on weekends. I had to work every weekend and holidays, which was rough, because a lot of times on holidays you want to go home to visit your family, that kind of thing. So there were times I couldn’t do that, and I was always playing music on the weekends. So I went to work from eight to five and then I would play a gig from maybe eight to twelve or nine to one, and get up on Sunday morning and go back to the hospital. So yeah, I paid a few dues. And before that actually in high school I was a shoe salesman and I washed dishes for one night at a chain called Bennigan’s Tavern. And luckily I had just auditioned for a disco band and the very day that I got hired to wash dishes I found out later that evening that they had hired me, the disco band decided that they wanted me to play with them. So I quit the job the next day.
Right. Well having those kinds of jobs helps keep things in perspective, doesn’t it?

Absolutely. Yeah. I think when we’re talking about playing music or being an artist of any kind, we’re talking about humility and humanity. And we have to remember that we’re communicating. When we’re performing we’re communicating with people who, 99% of your audience is nonmusicians. So we’re really trying to communicate to everybody. So sometimes as artists we tend to take these things for granted and what people do in their daily lives. So I think it really keeps us connected with that. Absolutely.
